svg.text: Customer Cohort Spend Evolution (Q1 Mini Data Platform)
Checkpoint 1: Storage Layer Architecture & Partition Layout (MinIO / S3) • Master SDBIS (FEAA, UAIC)
Core Question: "How does spend evolve for customers grouped by the month they first ordered?"
• Bîrgovan A. Mihai-Daniel (Ingest) • Schipor Ana-Maria (Tests & Quality)

g.text: • Max 2 containers running at a time
High Latency Per-Request / S3 HTTP API
[36 uniform monthly partitions spanning 3 full years]
• Avoids Small Files Problem on Object Storage
• Eliminates 2x GET round-trips per tiny file
(1 GET for file footer + 1 GET for data page)
DECISION D: WHY TABLE FORMAT FOR Q1?
• 40-Day Late Refunds mutate March net spend
• Zero dirty reads during background updates
dbt atomic table replacement inside DuckDB
• Direct HTTP Range requests over MinIO
• Late refunds restated against order month

svg.text: CHECKPOINT 1 MANDATORY DECISIONS SUMMARY (DEFENDED STRICTLY FOR Q1):
A. File Format (Parquet): Columnar projection pushdown reads only 4 columns
(customer_id, created_at, quantity, unit_price), saving >80% network I/O; rejected CSV & JSON.
B. Partition Key (sale_month): Matches Q1 monthly analytical grain, enables partition pruning
across 36 uniform partitions; rejected customer_id (119,975 tiny files = S3 metadata stall) and daily.
C. File Sizing (~1.2 MiB/month): Avoids S3 small-files HTTP latency penalty
(each file requires 2 GETs: footer + data). Coalesces writes, targeting 100-512 MiB in production.
D. Table Format (Iceberg / DuckLake): Warranted due to 40-day late refunds
mutating past months; provides ACID snapshots. Implemented via dbt DuckDB atomic swap (5 tools).
